paragraphs: The rapid scaling up of data center capacities, driven by emerging technology markets, pushes demand for raw materials. Every added megawatt embeds 60 - 75 tonnes of metals and minerals, mainly in power and cooling systems. To illustrate the scale, 200,000 tonnes of steel is required for a multi-building data center campus of 1.7 million square meters. In comparison Wembley football stadium required 23,000 tonnes of steel.
While copper, aluminum, and iron contribute the most in terms of kilograms per megawatt, data centers contribute the most to global demand of Gallium, Germanium and Tin.

Copper underpins all electrical infrastructure from battery storage systems to cooling systems in data centers to power grids. While demand for Copper surges, supply is projected to decrease in the coming decade due to declining ore grades and mounting geopolitical and environmental challenges. The average quality of copper ore being mined has dropped roughly 40% since the early 1990s. Because ore is less pure, it takes more time, energy, and water to extract the same amount of usable copper. The rate of new  large-scale copper discoveries has also plummeted, with few major deposits found in the last decade.
Many of the major mining regions such as Chile, Peru, and democratic republic of congo have faced compounding issues of severe droughts, earthquakes, localized flooding, and regulatory disputes.

Cobalt has unique magnetic and electrochemical properties that makes it an essential material for advanced semiconductor nodes, high-performance hardware components, and rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is the single-largest producer of mined cobalt, and contributes more than 70% of primary cobalt production. The extraction of cobalt, especially in the DRC, is often linked to hazardous working conditions, human exploitations, and severe environmental degradation.
While demand is expected to grow, Cobalt supply is expected to contract in the coming decade due to export restrictions by the DRC, price volatility, and other geopolitical factors.
